name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Thursday 23 October 1986

clue.text: Accidentally lit, some burn fast

indicators.note: an accident upsets the intended arrangement, so the letters following are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: every letter of these words is rearranged

explanation.surface: Things set alight by accident can go up very quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: it is the anagram and also a description of what happens when something catches fire unexpectedly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something accidentally set alight that burns fast suddenly catches fire all over, which is what bursting into flames describes.

clue.text: Eminence's good points

blocks.note: surface reading: the merits of a distinguished person; setter's reading: His Eminence is how a cardinal is addressed
setter's reading: virtues, so the phrase becomes a senior churchman's virtues

explanation.walkthrough: Cardinals of the Roman Catholic Church are styled 'His Eminence'. The four principal virtues of prudence, justice, temperance and fortitude carry the same adjective, from Latin cardo, a hinge.
explanation.definitionFit: The cardinal virtues are the chief moral good qualities, and a cardinal is addressed as Eminence, so they are an Eminence's good points.

clue.text: Leading desperate character to Church starts the ball rolling

blocks.note: leading in a race means in first place
Desperate Dan is the strongman of the British children's comic The Dandy
CE is the Church of England; 'to' adds it on the end

explanation.surface: Bringing a hardened criminal to church gets things moving.
explanation.walkthrough: Desperate Dan is a cowboy who eats cow pie in The Dandy, a long-running British comic. 'Ball' is the dance, not something round.
explanation.definitionFit: At a formal ball the first dance opens the evening's dancing, literally starting the ball off.

clue.text: Indian may be related to Russian

blocks.clueFragment: Indian may be related to Russian
blocks.note: surface reading: a claim about family links between peoples or languages of India and Russia
setter's reading: a Russian is a Red

explanation.walkthrough: Red was Cold War shorthand for a Russian communist. The answer is an old and now offensive term for a Native American, the 'Indian' here.
explanation.definitionFit: The word was once common, now offensive, slang for a North American Indian, from the supposed skin colour.

clue.text: Stonework for a student

blocks.note: op is short for opus, Latin for a work
taken as written
L is a learner, from the plates on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: Masonry as a project set for an apprentice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stonework' reads as one word; the definition is just its first half.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is a precious stone with a milky, shifting play of colours.

clue.text: Politician goes to dance with strikers for kicks

definitions.note: phrase standing for events at which balls are kicked

blocks.note: Michael Foot led the British Labour Party in the early 1980s
a ball is a formal dance
matches are struck to light them

explanation.surface: A politician spends an evening dancing alongside trade-union strikers, just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strikers' suggests football forwards or industrial action; it is what you strike for a light. 'For kicks' means for fun on the surface but here means where balls get kicked.
explanation.definitionFit: Football matches are games played by kicking a ball, so they are literally occasions for kicks.

clue.text: Cert? The old horse is lame - it might be used for a banquet!

definitions.text: it might be used for a banquet!

indicators.note: a lame horse cannot move properly, so the letters come out in a disordered new arrangement

blocks.note: every letter of these words is rearranged

explanation.surface: A racing tip on a sure thing goes wrong when the old nag turns out lame, so the horse may end up as banquet meat.
explanation.walkthrough: A cert is a racing certainty. The Dorchester is a grand hotel on Park Lane in London, known for its banqueting rooms.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dorchester Hotel hosts formal dinners and grand functions, so it is a venue used for a banquet.

clue.text: It's therapeutic to see the priest about tea-time

indicators.note: the priest stands about, that is around, the other piece, wrapping it on both sides

blocks.note: a curate is an assistant priest in a parish
tea-time is four o'clock, and four in Roman numerals is IV

explanation.surface: A visit to the vicar at tea-time is recommended as good for you.
explanation.walkthrough: Traditional British tea-time is four in the afternoon, and the clock-face numeral for four supplies the inner piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Something curative heals or restores health, which is exactly what a therapeutic remedy does.

clue.text: For a weight, it's not very big

blocks.note: pro is Latin for 'for', as in pros and cons
a ton is a unit of weight

explanation.surface: Someone is dismissing a weight as rather small.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is playful: a PROTON is a subatomic particle, about as far from very big as anything gets.
explanation.definitionFit: A proton is a tiny particle in the nucleus of an atom, so it is certainly not very big.

clue.text: They're not meant to be heard, like assassination date

definitions.text: They're not meant to be heard

blocks.note: as and like both mean 'in the manner of'
Julius Caesar was murdered on the Ides of March

explanation.surface: Whispered remarks about the date of a planned killing.
explanation.walkthrough: In a play, an aside is spoken to the audience and by convention the other characters on stage do not hear it.
explanation.definitionFit: Asides are stage remarks the other characters are supposed not to hear, so they are not meant to be heard.

clue.text: Closet is out of order for a long day or a long night

definitions.text: a long day or a long night

indicators.note: things out of order are not in their proper sequence, so the letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A broken cupboard door means the whole day or night drags on.
explanation.definitionFit: The summer solstice gives the longest day of the year and the winter solstice the longest night.

clue.text: Look said to signify

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the next word counts by its sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: to mean something is to signify it

explanation.surface: Someone claims a glance can convey meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Mien is a person's look or bearing, especially the expression that shows their mood.

clue.text: Dare I apply for work on the Guardian, for example?

indicators.note: to work something is to knead or shape it, so the letters are moulded into a new order

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A nervous job-seeker wonders whether to apply for a post at the Guardian newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apply for work' reads as one phrase about job-hunting; 'work' is in fact the signal to rearrange 'Dare I apply'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Guardian is a British newspaper published every day, so it is an example of a daily paper.

clue.text: Youth leader soon split . payment for the premises

indicators.note: a leader goes at the front, so only the opening letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the leader of youth is its first letter
early and soon both mean before long or before time
rent is a past tense of rend, to tear apart

explanation.surface: A youth-club leader is soon going to split from the group.
explanation.definitionFit: A yearly rent is the annual sum a tenant pays for occupying premises.

clue.text: Touch of fashion Heather gives to squalid accommodation

blocks.note: a sty is a pigsty, a byword for filthy lodgings
ling is a common name for heather

explanation.surface: A woman called Heather brings a bit of chic to a run-down flat.
explanation.walkthrough: Heather looks like a woman's name but is the plant. 'Gives to' means the heather is added on after the pigsty.
explanation.definitionFit: Styling is the finishing work that gives hair, clothes or a room a fashionable touch.

clue.text: Battles to obtain medication

indicators.note: the letters of battles are worked on in order to obtain the wanted word; a loose signal to rearrange

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone has to fight hard to get their prescription filled.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram signal is weak here; 'to obtain' has to be read as 'are rearranged to obtain'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tablets are pills, the most common form in which medication is taken.

clue.text: Sick in the sharp end? It's the waves!

indicators.note: in places the first idea inside the second, which wraps around it

blocks.note: ill means sick
the bows are the pointed front of a ship

explanation.surface: A seasick passenger at the front of the boat blames the rough sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The sharp end' is sailors' slang for the front of a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Billows are great rolling waves of the sea.

clue.text: Clerical lass comes in from the cold?

definitions.text: Clerical lass comes in from the cold?

blocks.note: surface reading: a young woman of the church, a clergyman's daughter perhaps
setter's reading: clerical means doing clerks' work, and she comes indoors to a desk job

explanation.walkthrough: 'Clerical' suggests the clergy and 'comes in from the cold' suggests a spy story; really it is a young clerk who works indoors.
explanation.definitionFit: An office girl is a young woman doing clerical work, typing and filing, inside a warm workplace.

clue.text: First class transport, with good ventilation

blocks.note: A1 means first-class, with the 1 written as the letter I
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A first-class train carriage advertised as well aired.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 was the top rating in Lloyd's Register of ships, hence first-class; the digit 1 stands in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: An airy room has plenty of fresh air moving through it, which is good ventilation.

clue.text: Charge of 22, or Father - a saint, it's said...

definitions.note: adjective as in pastoral charge, the care of souls a rector holds

blocks.note: pa is an informal word for father
St is the standard abbreviation for saint
oral means spoken rather than written

explanation.surface: A rector's flock, or a father and a saint, as the saying goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is RECTOR; a rector's care for his parishioners is his pastoral charge. 'It's said' supplies a word meaning spoken, not a sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastoral describes a clergyman's spiritual care of his congregation, the charge entrusted to a rector.

clue.text: Minister set 'up to be a prophet

indicators.note: in a down entry, set up means read from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: a seer is someone who foresees the future

explanation.surface: A government minister is installed and hailed as a visionary.
explanation.walkthrough: Merlyn Rees was a British Labour cabinet minister, Home Secretary from 1976 to 1979. The stray quote mark is in the printed clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Merlyn Rees held several posts in British Labour governments, so the surname names a minister of the day.

clue.text: . Father, if in correct orders

indicators.note: in says the wanted word sits inside the following phrase, spanning the gap between its two words

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A priest is properly a Father only if he has been ordained into holy orders.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue continues the ellipsis from 20 and reads as a remark on ordination; 'orders' suggests holy orders but simply supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A rector is a parish priest, and priests are addressed as Father.

clue.text: Cut by a quarter -that's serious!

blocks.note: to sever is to cut through
east is one of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: A cut of a quarter of something is no small matter.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass has four quarters, N, S, E and W, so 'a quarter' can stand for any one of them; 'by' means placed beside.
explanation.definitionFit: Severe means grave or serious, as of an illness, injury or punishment.

clue.text: Erratic person warned off by the queen

indicators.note: off means gone wrong or out of kilter, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters to be rearranged
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen

explanation.surface: An unpredictable courtier is told by Her Majesty to keep away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Warned off' reads as a single verb, but 'off' is the signal for 'warned' alone.
explanation.definitionFit: Erratic comes from Latin for wandering, so an erratic person who drifts about is a wanderer.
